words.intro: Every German block of flats now has a group chat. It was started to share parcels. Six months later, it has rules, a splinter group, and a very formal letter about a bicycle.

grammar[0].fact: German firms often have an informal *du* culture now, and yet a German email to someone outside still begins *Sehr geehrte*. There’s a middle: *Guten Tag, Frau Weber*, which has become the safest start of all. And *Hallo* to a stranger may or may not get a reply.

grammar[1].fact: German online forums have a rule, and it is older than most of the internet: *Netiquette*. German courts have taken an interest too, and a hateful post can bring a fine. Some newspapers close their comment sections overnight, when there’s nobody awake to check them.

document.intro: A real sign at a fairground ride, and it’s the most German thing there is: a ghost train with a *Hausordnung*. Blood drips from the title, and below it, in perfectly formal German, are the rules.
document.fact: Notice the warning *es kann gruselig werden*, it may get scary. On a ghost train. *Den Anweisungen des Personals ist Folge zu leisten* is word for word what you’d read in any German office, swimming pool or train.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Say each rule in a chat voice, with du.
reading.intro: The group chat of Hofstraße 12 has 34 members. Lena set it up, for the parcels. Frau Huber has now joined, on a phone that Maya gave her. She has never been in a chat before. She doesn’t know that nobody writes letters in them.
reading.fact: Written German has two very different grammars now: a chat uses *du*, no capitals, and little punctuation, and a letter has rules from another century. A *du* on a work chat doesn’t always mean a *du* in the corridor. If in doubt, read the last message and copy it.
